strengths: The integration of ten heterogeneous facial analysis tasks addresses a useful computer vision systems problem. A shared model covering segmentation, geometry, attributes, and identity could simplify deployment and dataset annotation.

Evaluation covers numerous benchmarks and both specialized and multi-task baselines. Strong reported results include 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 NME on the full 300W test set, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. The 300VW Category-C result provides encouraging evidence of cross-dataset generalization.

Table 7 provides evidence that bidirectional attention helps: head-pose MAE improves from 4.63 to 3.52 relative to standard cross-attention. The reported 33.21 FPS and reduced parameter count relative to Faceptor also suggest a useful efficiency contribution.

The architecture overview is understandable, standard losses and datasets are cited, and the appendix supplies substantial augmentation details. Acknowledging recognition tradeoffs and examining demographic performance are appropriate.
weaknesses: The central architectural novelty is insufficiently established. The decoder closely resembles SAM’s two-way transformer: token self-attention, token-to-image attention, image-to-token attention, and a final token-to-image update. SAM [40] is cited generically, but this architectural relationship is not discussed. The paper should distinguish its facial-task integration contribution from previously introduced decoder mechanisms.

The claimed resolution of incompatible preprocessing is not demonstrated convincingly. Section 3.4 motivates unification around this problem, yet Appendices F.2 and F.7 retain five-point alignment for landmarks and recognition, while head pose uses loose crops. The manuscript needs to establish that one fixed checkpoint and a common inference input deliver the reported results simultaneously, including recognition.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the proposed mechanism’s contribution. There is no matched shared-backbone baseline with ordinary task heads or single-task counterparts, and component ablations cover only four tasks. Efficiency comparisons also change the backbone, resolution, and decoder architecture together, so they cannot attribute the speed advantage specifically to bidirectional attention. Inference hardware and batch size should be specified.

Quantitative evidence contains a consequential reporting inconsistency: the ten FaceXFormer class scores in Table 3 average to 91.01, not 92.01. This leaves a 0.12-point lead over Faceptor’s 90.89 rather than the reported 1.12-point lead. The result remains promising, but the headline improvement needs correction. Additionally, no quantitative race-estimation result substantiates that component of the ten-task claim.

Important reproduction details remain unresolved: loss weights, treatment of missing task labels, and the tasks and parameter updates involved in the additional three training epochs are unspecified. Appendix F.5 introduces MORPH-II training and evaluation, whereas the main protocol and age-results table identify UTKFace; the actual datasets, splits, and label harmonization need reconciliation.

The bias analysis does not support the broad claim of minimal bias. Table 8’s age discrepancy is 0.50, larger than CLIP’s absolute 0.30 and FaRL’s 0.35, while average age accuracy is lower. Pooling six populations into one non-white group can conceal disparities, and no ablation establishes that race co-training causes the reported parity. The analysis is welcome, but its conclusions should be narrowed.
